summary: One God in three persons; the eternal relations of Father, Son, and Spirit
readingInstruction: Read Deuteronomy 6:4, Matthew 28:18-20, and 2 Corinthians 13:14. Today is a doctrinal pause on the Trinity. Notice that Deuteronomy says God is one, and the two New Testament verses name the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together.
settingTheScene: The Bible never uses the word “Trinity,” but it teaches the truth the word describes. In Deuteronomy, Israel confesses, “The LORD our God, the LORD is one.” In the Great Commission, Jesus tells us to baptize in the singular “name” of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Paul ends 2 Corinthians with a blessing that names all three. The church has summarized this teaching in its creeds.
observation: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4).
“Baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).
“All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18).
“Teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:20).
“And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).
“The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 13:14).
“And the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Corinthians 13:14).
doctrinalFocus: The Trinity is the biblical teaching that there is one God who eternally exists as three distinct persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who are each fully God, and who share one divine essence. The persons are not three gods, and they are not three modes or masks of one person. The Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Spirit, and the Spirit is not the Father, yet there is one God. The persons are equal in glory and eternal, and they relate to one another in love: the Father eternally begets the Son, and the Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father and the Son. In salvation, the Father plans and sends, the Son accomplishes redemption, and the Spirit applies it.
interpretation:
Start with Deuteronomy 6:4, the Shema. Israel’s creed was that the LORD is one. In a world of many gods, this was the foundation of Israel’s faith. The New Testament does not abandon it. Instead it reveals that this one God has a fuller inner life than Israel knew.

In Matthew 28:19, Jesus commands baptism “in the name” (singular) of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. A single name for three persons, side by side, as equals. If the Son and the Spirit were mere creatures, to place them alongside the Father in this way would be blasphemy. Jesus also claims “all authority in heaven and on earth,” and promises to be present everywhere with his people always, which only God can do.

In 2 Corinthians 13:14, Paul names the three together in a blessing. He does not explain it, but assumes it. The blessing is the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. Each person gives something, and all are equally God. Similar patterns appear throughout the New Testament, at Jesus’ baptism (the Father speaks, the Son is baptized, the Spirit descends), and in Ephesians 1, where the Father chooses, the Son redeems, and the Spirit seals.

Why does this matter? First, it means that God is love in himself. Before creation, the Father, Son, and Spirit shared perfect love. God did not need us to be loving. Second, it means that salvation is the work of the whole Trinity. Third, it means that when we worship Jesus, we are not violating monotheism, and when we pray by the Spirit we are speaking with God. The doctrine is a mystery, something we receive and adore, not something we fully comprehend. But it is the shape of the gospel.
connection: John 1:1-3 and 14 reveal the Word who was with God and was God. John 14:16-17 mentions the Father, Son, and the Spirit as another Helper. Genesis 1:26 says “Let us make man.” Matthew 3:16-17 shows all three at Jesus’ baptism. Ephesians 1:3-14 sets out the work of each person. Romans 8:9-11 speaks of the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ. 1 Peter 1:2. Isaiah 6:8. Hebrews 9:14.
application:
Pray to each person of the Trinity this week: thank the Father for his love, the Son for his grace, and the Spirit for his fellowship.

Use the blessing in 2 Corinthians 13:14 to end a prayer or bless a loved one.

Resist the urge to reduce the Trinity to a neat illustration. Worship the mystery.
prayerPrompts: Worship the Father, Son, and Spirit, one God, in your own words.
Thank the Father for his love, the Son for his grace, and the Spirit for his fellowship.
Ask them to help you know each more.
